transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you. It’s, ah... it’s a bit difficult to put into words, to be perfectly honest with you. I’ve spent the better part of the last few weeks just debating whether I should even make this appointment. You see, I’ve always been a very practical man. Going all the way back to my graduate studies, and then throughout my entire career, I was the sort of person who believed that if you just put your head down, made a schedule, and applied a bit of rigor, you could overcome just about any hurdle. 

But lately, especially since I’ve stepped away from the workforce, things have shifted. I came in today because I’ve started to feel—and it’s not some sudden, dramatic crisis, but rather in a very quiet, incredibly stubborn way—that the best version of my life is simply behind me. It's this heavy, persistent realization that no amount of planning or discipline on my part is going to get me back to feeling like myself. I used to be able to logic my way out of a rut, to just organize my days better, but now I just keep looking at the years ahead and thinking that the good chapters are already written and closed. And I just don't know what to do with that feeling, because my usual tools for fixing things just aren't working anymore.
Have you been feeling sad or empty most of the time lately?

Sad... well, it's not quite like the sadness you might expect. I mean, I’m not breaking down in tears or having these dramatic, weeping moments. I’ve never really been that sort of person anyway, even when things were genuinely tough. But empty... yes, maybe empty is closer to the mark, or perhaps just... muted. 

Most days, it’s like there is this... this low, gray tone running underneath absolutely everything I do. And I do mean everything. It doesn't seem to matter what the activity is or how much I try to apply myself to it. I could be out in my studio—I try to spend time out there, just tinkering and trying to stay busy, keeping my hands moving to maintain some semblance of a routine now that I'm retired—and that gray feeling is just sitting right there on the workbench with me. 

Or even in the evenings, which is what really bothers me the most, if I'm being honest. I'll be sitting right across the table from my wife at dinner. She’s a wonderful woman, and she’ll be talking about her day, or the neighbors, or whatever is going on with our friends, and I’m looking at her, and I know I should be engaged. I know I should feel that normal warmth of a shared meal. But instead, that dull, heavy grayness is just... it's just humming along in the background, completely ignoring the fact that I'm supposed to be enjoying a nice evening. It’s almost like someone turned down the color saturation on my entire life, and I just can't seem to find the dial to turn it back up, no matter how hard I concentrate on the meal or the conversation.
Do you find that you're no longer enjoying activities that you used to find pleasurable?

Well, it's... it's a complicated question, isn't it? Because "pleasure" is such a strong word. I wouldn't say I've stopped doing things, exactly. Like I mentioned, I still go out to the studio. I have a whole setup out there—woodworking tools I’ve collected over the better part of three decades, a really beautiful lathe that I used to spend hours on, just turning bowls and table legs. I used to lose track of time out there. I'd go out after breakfast and suddenly my wife would be calling me in for supper, and I'd realize I hadn't even stopped for lunch. 

I still go out there. I make it a point to go out there every morning at nine o'clock, right after I finish my coffee and the morning paper. I put on my apron, I select a piece of wood—maybe a nice piece of cherry or walnut—and I turn on the equipment. But... the feeling just isn't the same. I'm going through the motions, applying the chisels, sanding the grain down, but that sense of satisfaction, that quiet thrill of seeing something take shape under my hands... it's just not there. I finish a bowl, I set it on the shelf with the others, and I just feel... nothing in particular about it. 

And it's not just the woodworking. I used to really enjoy reading history biographies. I have a whole library of them in the den. I'd get so absorbed in the political maneuvering of the 19th century, or the strategic decisions during the World Wars. Now, I can sit in my favorite leather chair, open a book about Churchill or Lincoln, and I might read ten pages before I realize I haven't absorbed a single word. I'm just looking at the letters on the page. The interest, the spark that used to make me want to turn the page and see what happens next, even though I already know the history... it's just absent. So, I suppose I'm still doing the activities, but the enjoyment I used to extract from them... that seems to have evaporated somewhere along the line, despite my best efforts to keep up the routine.
How long have you been feeling this way, with this gray, muted tone to your life?

Well, that’s... that’s a very good question, and one I’ve actually spent quite a bit of time trying to pinpoint myself. Because, as I said, it wasn't a sudden drop-off. It wasn't like waking up one morning and finding the world had lost its color. It was much more insidious than that. 

But if I really trace it back, if I look at the timeline of when things started to feel like a chore rather than a life... it goes back to a hiking trip. My wife and I used to be quite active, you see. We loved the trails up in the state park, the ones with the really steep inclines that give you that wonderful view of the valley. We'd go every autumn when the leaves were turning. But a little over three years ago—it was October, so about three years and three months ago now, to be precise—I took a bad step on a loose rock coming down the ridge. 

It was a silly mistake, really. I had good boots on, I was using my poles, but I just lost my footing. I ended up with a rather nasty injury to my knee. Nothing life-threatening, of course, but it required surgery and a very, very long, tedious physical therapy process. And I remember sitting in that recliner in our living room with my leg elevated on these two specific pillows my wife bought just for that purpose, watching the snow fall outside that winter, and realizing I couldn't get out to my studio. I couldn't walk the dog. I couldn't do much of anything except read, and as I mentioned, even that started to lose its appeal. 

And that’s when I think this... this grayness really settled in. I kept telling myself, "Once the knee heals, once you're back on your feet, the fog will lift." And the knee did heal, eventually. I mean, it still aches when it rains, but I can walk perfectly fine now. But the fog... the fog never lifted. It just stayed right there, long after the physical therapy appointments ended. So yes, it’s been a little over three years now that I’ve been carrying this around with me. Three years of just... going through the motions.
Do you often find yourself feeling guilty or reproaching yourself for things that have happened or for your current situation?

Guilty? No, I wouldn't say guilty. It's not like I'm sitting around beating myself up over the past or feeling like I've committed some great wrong. I mean, I certainly have regrets, as I'm sure any man my age does—you don't get to be sixty-five without wishing you'd handled a few things differently along the way. Like that time back in '98 when I decided not to take that partnership offer at the firm because I thought the commute would be too taxing, and then the firm ended up expanding massively... but that's just life, isn't it? That's not what you're asking about. 

As for my current situation, this... this muted feeling... I don't feel guilty about it. It's more of a frustration, really. A profound, quiet frustration. I know my wife gets worried, and I suppose I feel a twinge of regret that I can't be the lively companion she married, the one who used to plan all those hiking trips and surprise her with weekend getaways to bed and breakfasts up the coast. But guilt implies I feel like I'm doing this on purpose, or that it's a moral failing on my part. And I don't think it is. I'm trying, you know? I'm going out to the studio every morning at nine, I'm sitting down for dinner, I'm attempting to read my biographies. I'm doing everything I'm supposed to do to keep the engine running, so to speak. It's just that the engine isn't producing any power. So no, I don't sit in my leather chair reproaching myself. I just sit there wondering why the effort I'm putting in isn't yielding any sort of return.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

Well, that’s the rub, isn't it? I’ve been racking my brain trying to find something—anything, really—that sparks that old feeling. You’d think, being retired, having all this free time and a comfortable pension, I’d be jumping out of bed to seize the day. 

Take my daughter, for example. She comes over most Sunday afternoons with our two grandchildren. Now, any grandfather worth his salt is supposed to look forward to that all week, right? My wife spends two days prepping for it, baking cookies, getting a roast ready—the whole house smells like rosemary and garlic by noon on Sunday. And the kids, they come bursting through the front door, the dog gets all riled up and starts barking, it’s this whole grand production. It’s exactly the sort of family picture I worked all those decades at the firm to be able to sit back and enjoy in my twilight years. 

But... if I'm being completely honest with you, and I suppose that's why I'm sitting in this office... I don't actually look forward to it. I see it marked on the calendar in the kitchen, and instead of anticipation, I just feel... well, tired, I suppose. I think about the noise, and the sheer amount of energy it’s going to require to sit there and smile and ask the boys about their little league games and pretend I'm engaged. I love them, obviously. I'm not a monster, I care for my family deeply. But that actual feeling of joy? That little flutter in your chest when you know something good is about to happen? I just don't have it. 

And it's the same for the little things, too. I used to love just walking down the driveway to get the mail. I'd enjoy the crisp morning air, maybe chat with Bob, our postman—he's been on our route for fifteen years, good man, his son just graduated from state college. But now, even walking down the driveway is just a chore. It's just another thing I have to do. Not for Sunday dinners, not for my woodworking, not even for a quiet evening on the porch with a glass of iced tea. It’s all just... tasks on a list now. Boxes to check before the sun goes down. So, no, to answer your question. I really can't think of a single thing I genuinely look forward to anymore.
Have you noticed a decrease in your ability to experience pleasure from activities you once enjoyed?

Well, I'm... I'm not entirely sure what you mean by that, doctor, or how that's fundamentally different from what we were just discussing. I mean, I feel like I just answered that, didn't I? I just told you all about the Sunday dinners with my daughter and the grandchildren, and how I don't get any joy out of them anymore. So if you're asking if there's been a decrease... well, yes, obviously. That's the whole crux of the matter. That's the gray, muted tone I've been trying to explain to you since I first sat down in this chair. 

I really don't have any new or different examples to give you, if that's what you're looking for. I've already walked you through how I go out to my woodworking studio and just sit there without actually wanting to make anything. I've told you about the family visits, the morning walks to the mailbox to see Bob... I haven't noticed any *other* specific areas of decrease, if that's what you're fishing for, because it feels like the decrease has already painted over everything I do. It's just a general, overarching lack of enjoyment in the very things I spent my entire career at the firm looking forward to doing in my retirement. 

So, I'm not sure I can give you a better or more specific answer than the one I just gave you a moment ago. The pleasure is just... it's just not there. Across the board. I hope that makes sense, because I'm really not sure how else to explain it to you.
Are there any activities, no matter how small, that you still find give you some sense of pleasure?

Doctor, I... I have to admit, I'm starting to feel like a broken record here, and I'm wondering if maybe I'm just not speaking clearly enough. We are essentially circling the exact same drain. When you say "no matter how small," I really did mean it when I said I've already thought about the little things. I mentioned the walk to the mailbox. I mentioned sitting with a glass of iced tea. 

But, alright, if we really need to drill down into the absolute minutiae of my day to be absolutely certain... let me walk you through it. Let's take an average Tuesday morning. I wake up. I go to the kitchen. I take out the coffee grinder. My wife buys these very nice, expensive Ethiopian beans from a little specialty roaster downtown—the one over by the old courthouse, you might know it. Used to be, just opening that bag and smelling the roast was a... well, a tiny little highlight. A thirty-second moment of genuine pleasure before the day began. Now? It's just noise. The grinder is just a loud noise, and the coffee is just a hot liquid I swallow out of sheer habit. 

Then I sit down with the morning paper. I used to get a real kick out of reading the editorial section, you know, really dissecting the op-eds. I spent forty years doing corporate litigation, so picking apart a poorly structured argument used to be my bread and butter. I'd read some politician's nonsense and feel a little spark of intellectual superiority, I suppose you could say. But now? I just look at the words. I read them, I comprehend them, and I feel absolutely nothing. I don't care enough to argue with the newspaper. I just fold it up and put it in the recycling bin. 

So, to answer your question for what feels like the third time... no. Not the big things like the grandchildren, not the medium things like my woodworking studio, and not the small things like the smell of expensive coffee or a well-written article. Nothing. I really don't know how else to explain it to you, doctor. Every single activity, regardless of its size or significance, is just completely flat.
Do you often feel tired or lacking in energy?

Well, yes. Yes, I do. But it’s... it’s a peculiar kind of tired, if I’m being precise. It’s not that I’m bedridden or incapable of functioning, so please don't get the wrong impression. I still get up at the same time every morning. I still do my share of the household errands—I do the grocery shopping on Tuesdays and Thursdays, for instance. My wife always insists I’m the one who goes because she claims I have a better eye for picking out the produce, which is rather ironic considering I spent forty years looking at legal briefs, not heirloom tomatoes. 

And, as I mentioned before, I still go out to the garage and tinker with my woodworking projects. I go through the motions. But the energy it takes to do these things... it’s entirely disproportionate to the task itself. 

Let me give you an example. I do a bit of volunteer mentoring for some of the local law students—just trying to pass on some practical knowledge about corporate litigation that they don't teach you in a textbook. It used to be effortless. Now, just the process of setting up for a mentoring session... arranging the chairs, making sure I have my notes in order, greeting the students... it leaves me completely worn out. Or if my wife wants to go to one of those community events they hold downtown in the square—the art fairs or the farmer's market—just walking through the event, navigating the stalls and the people... by the time we get back to the car, I feel like I've just argued a grueling three-week trial. 

And the frustrating part is that resting doesn't seem to cure it. I’ll come home from one of these outings, sit down in my recliner in the den, and try to sleep it off. But even if I do manage to drift off, a nap doesn’t really fix it. I wake up feeling just as heavy and drained as I did before I closed my eyes. It’s this persistent, bone-deep weariness that just follows me around, no matter what I’m doing or how much I rest.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities that you used to enjoy?

Doctor, I... honestly, I am completely baffled as to why we are circling back to this yet again. I feel like we are trapped in some sort of deposition where the opposing counsel just keeps asking the same question in slightly different ways, hoping I'll somehow give a different answer. 

Have I lost interest in activities I used to enjoy? Yes, doctor. I have. We've spent the better part of this session discussing exactly that. I told you about the Sunday dinners with my daughter and the grandchildren. I told you about my woodworking studio out in the garage, and how I just sit there staring at the tools. I told you about the morning walks to the mailbox to see Bob. I walked you through the minutiae of grinding the Ethiopian coffee beans and reading the editorial section of the morning paper. 

So, yes, the interest is gone. The enjoyment is gone. It's all just... flat. It's a chore. I don't know how many different ways I can describe this overarching grayness to you. It feels like I've exhausted every possible example from my daily life, from the major family events down to the thirty seconds it takes to grind coffee beans. I'm really trying to be cooperative here, but I'm struggling to understand what nuance you're looking for that I haven't already provided three or four times now.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Well, no, not really. Sleep itself isn't the problem, not in the sense of... well, you know, tossing and turning or staring at the ceiling until three in the morning. I don't have insomnia, if that's what you're getting at. 

I actually keep a very strict schedule. I always have. Forty years in corporate litigation will drill that into you—you have to be disciplined with your time or the work just swallows you whole. So, my wife and I, we head up to the bedroom around ten o'clock every night. She usually reads one of her mystery novels for a bit—she goes through those paperbacks like water, I swear she buys three new ones every week at that little used bookstore on Elm Street. I might look over some notes for my mentoring sessions, or just close my eyes. And usually, by ten-thirty, the lights are out and I'm asleep. 

I sleep through the night, for the most part. Occasional trip to the bathroom, as you'd expect at my age, but I go right back to sleep. And I wake up at six-thirty, sharp, every morning. The alarm goes off, and I'm awake. 

So the mechanics of sleeping are perfectly intact. I get my eight hours. It's just that, as I was trying to explain earlier when we were talking about my energy levels... the sleep doesn't seem to *do* anything anymore. It used to be restorative, you know? You have a long day, you get a good night's sleep, and you wake up feeling refreshed and ready to tackle the next set of depositions or whatever was on the docket. Now, I sleep the full eight hours, I dream, I wake up, and I feel exactly as heavy and drained as I did when I laid down. It's like plugging in a phone overnight and waking up to find the battery is still at ten percent. 

But to answer your specific question about having *trouble* sleeping... no. Getting to sleep and staying asleep isn't an issue at all. I just wish the sleep actually accomplished something.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

No, no, I haven't lost any weight. My weight has been remarkably stable, actually. I've hovered right around a hundred and eighty-five pounds for the better part of the last decade. It's one of the few things that hasn't changed. 

You know, my wife, she keeps a very close eye on what we eat. She got onto this Mediterranean diet kick about five years ago after her brother had a mild scare with his cholesterol. So our meals are very structured—lots of grilled fish, olive oil, leafy greens. We used to go out to dinner at least twice a week when I was still at the firm, usually to this Italian place near the courthouse, Luigi's. I'd always get the veal parmesan, which I'm sure wasn't doing my arteries any favors. But now, it's mostly home-cooked meals. 

And as I mentioned, the enjoyment of the food is completely gone. I sit down to dinner, and it just tastes like... well, like cardboard, quite frankly. I chew, I swallow, I go through the motions because I know I need the sustenance, and because my wife went to the trouble of preparing it. I don't want to upset her by refusing to eat. She puts so much effort into finding these recipes—she even started growing her own herbs in little pots on the kitchen windowsill. Basil, thyme, rosemary. She’s very proud of them. 

So, I eat what's put in front of me. I clean my plate, just like I always have. The mechanics of eating, much like the mechanics of sleeping, haven't changed. I just don't get any satisfaction from it anymore. But to answer your question, no, the scale hasn't budged. My suits all still fit exactly the same way they did when I retired. I suppose that's a small mercy, not having to go out and buy a whole new wardrobe, but... well, no, no weight loss to speak of.
Do you find yourself wanting to be around other people less often than you used to?

Well, yes. Yes, I suppose that's the long and short of it. I just... I don't have the bandwidth for it anymore. It's not that I actively dislike people all of a sudden, or that I'm sitting here nursing some profound misanthropy. It's just the sheer effort of it all. 

I mean, I still manage the basics around the house. I talk to my wife, obviously. I'll exchange pleasantries with the mail carrier if we happen to cross paths, though as I mentioned earlier, even that morning walk has lost its appeal. But beyond the absolute bare minimum, yes, I've pulled back considerably. 

Take my mentoring, for example. I used to really enjoy that. Working with the junior associates, reviewing their briefs, teaching them the finer points of deposition strategy... it gave me a sense of purpose. I was passing the torch, so to speak. I had a regular group of three or four young lawyers I'd meet with every Tuesday afternoon at this little coffee shop near the firm. But I just... I couldn't keep up the facade. Sitting there, trying to muster enthusiasm for contract disputes when everything just feels so gray and heavy... I eventually just told them I needed to take an indefinite hiatus. I said it was for personal reasons, which I suppose is true enough.

And it's not just the professional stuff. We used to be quite active in the community. My wife and I were on the organizing committee for the annual summer festival at the park down the street. I used to coordinate the local music gatherings—booking the jazz quartets, making sure the staging was right. I haven't been to a single committee meeting in months. I just let my wife go on her own, or she skips it entirely, which makes me feel guilty, but I just can't bring myself to sit in a room with twelve other people debating whether to hire a face painter or a balloon artist. 

Even our travel plans... we had talked about taking a river cruise through Europe this fall. The Danube, I think it was. We had the brochures sitting on the kitchen counter for weeks. But the thought of navigating airports, making small talk with other couples at dinner, pretending to be awestruck by castles... I just couldn't do it. I told her we should postpone. 

So, yes, my weeks are much, much smaller than they used to be. My world has basically shrunk down to the walls of my house. And even then, I find myself retreating to the garage or the den just to be alone. It's just easier that way. You don't have to pretend when you're by yourself.
Have you ever thought about harming yourself or wished you were dead?

No, no. Heavens, no. I want to be very clear about that right out of the gate. I haven't had any thoughts of... of harming myself, or wishing I wouldn't wake up, or anything of that nature. 

I know I've been sitting here for the better part of this appointment painting a rather bleak picture of my day-to-day existence—the lack of energy, pulling away from the festival committee and my mentoring group, the dinners tasting like cardboard. I suppose when you stack all of that together on a notepad, it probably sounds like someone who has just given up completely. But there is a very distinct line, in my mind anyway, between feeling like a drained battery and actually wanting to... well, to throw the battery away entirely, if you follow my meaning. 

I spent forty years in corporate litigation, as I mentioned before. You see a lot of people in incredibly high-stress situations, and sadly, over the decades, I've known a couple of colleagues who did go down that very dark path. There was a senior partner back in the late eighties—brilliant man, absolutely brilliant mind for antitrust law—who just couldn't take it anymore. I saw firsthand what that did to his family. The absolute, unimaginable devastation it left behind for his wife and his children. The messy aftermath of it all. 

I could never, ever do that to my wife. She’s... well, she’s the one keeping our routine going right now, isn't she? Cooking those Mediterranean meals, tending to her little basil and thyme plants on the windowsill, trying to keep things normal. To inflict that kind of trauma on her? Unthinkable. Absolutely unthinkable. I take my commitments very seriously, and my marriage is the most important one I have. 

So, no. I don't wish I were dead. I just wish... I just wish I felt *alive* again, the way I used to. Right now, I'm just enduring. I wake up at six-thirty sharp, I go through the motions, I eat what's put in front of me, and I fulfill my basic obligations. It's a very flat, gray sort of endurance. Just putting one foot in front of the other. But it *is* endurance. I have absolutely no intention of cutting it short. I suppose I'm just waiting for the color to come back to things, even if I don't quite know how to make that happen right now. But as far as harming myself goes, no. Not at all.
How many months or years have you been feeling this persistent, low, gray tone in your life?

Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... it’s been quite a while. It's funny you use the word 'gray,' because that's exactly how it feels. If I had to put a pin in the calendar, I'd say this all really settled in right after a hiking injury I had. 

My wife and I, before all of this, we used to love going up to the state park on weekends. We had this one particular trail we'd do, not too strenuous, but enough to get the heart rate up and get some fresh air. Anyway, I want to say it was early spring, because the ground was still a bit slick from the thaw, and I took a bad step on some loose rock. I ended up with a rather nasty hiking injury. It was quite a production getting me down from the ridge, let me tell you. 

I had to be off my feet for quite a while after that, doing all the tedious rehabilitation exercises, sitting in my armchair with ice packs while my wife fussed over me. And I suppose... well, the physical injury healed eventually. I can walk perfectly fine now, as I mentioned with my morning strolls. But that vitality, that spark I had before the fall? It just never returned. The grayness just sort of crept in while I was laid up in that chair, and it simply never lifted. 

So, if I'm doing the math correctly, that hiking injury was a little over three years ago. Yes, about three years and three months now, to be precise. Three years and three months. It sounds a bit like a prison sentence when you say it out loud like that, doesn't it? Thirty-nine months of just... going through the motions. You'd think at some point over the course of a thousand days, you'd wake up and the sky would look blue again, but it just stays that same flat, overcast color. 

I remember my wife bought me this thousand-piece jigsaw puzzle of the Amalfi coast to do while I was recovering from the injury, trying to keep my mind sharp since I couldn't go into the office. I did the buildings, the boats, but I just couldn't bring myself to finish the sky because all the blue pieces just looked entirely identical to me. I just stared at them and felt absolutely exhausted by the prospect of trying to fit them together. I suppose that was a bit of a metaphor, in hindsight. But yes, to answer your question, it's been exactly that long. Three years and three months of this.

doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Hopelessness
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I’ve started to feel, in a quiet but stubborn way, that the best version of my life is behind me and that no amount of planning or discipline is going to get me back to feeling like myself.

patient.answer:
Well, thank you. It’s, ah... it’s a bit difficult to put into words, to be perfectly honest with you. I’ve spent the better part of the last few weeks just debating whether I should even make this appointment. You see, I’ve always been a very practical man. Going all the way back to my graduate studies, and then throughout my entire career, I was the sort of person who believed that if you just put your head down, made a schedule, and applied a bit of rigor, you could overcome just about any hurdle. 

But lately, especially since I’ve stepped away from the workforce, things have shifted. I came in today because I’ve started to feel—and it’s not some sudden, dramatic crisis, but rather in a very quiet, incredibly stubborn way—that the best version of my life is simply behind me. It's this heavy, persistent realization that no amount of planning or discipline on my part is going to get me back to feeling like myself. I used to be able to logic my way out of a rut, to just organize my days better, but now I just keep looking at the years ahead and thinking that the good chapters are already written and closed. And I just don't know what to do with that feeling, because my usual tools for fixing things just aren't working anymore.

patient.answer:
Well, that’s... that’s a very good question, and one I’ve actually spent quite a bit of time trying to pinpoint myself. Because, as I said, it wasn't a sudden drop-off. It wasn't like waking up one morning and finding the world had lost its color. It was much more insidious than that. 

But if I really trace it back, if I look at the timeline of when things started to feel like a chore rather than a life... it goes back to a hiking trip. My wife and I used to be quite active, you see. We loved the trails up in the state park, the ones with the really steep inclines that give you that wonderful view of the valley. We'd go every autumn when the leaves were turning. But a little over three years ago—it was October, so about three years and three months ago now, to be precise—I took a bad step on a loose rock coming down the ridge. 

It was a silly mistake, really. I had good boots on, I was using my poles, but I just lost my footing. I ended up with a rather nasty injury to my knee. Nothing life-threatening, of course, but it required surgery and a very, very long, tedious physical therapy process. And I remember sitting in that recliner in our living room with my leg elevated on these two specific pillows my wife bought just for that purpose, watching the snow fall outside that winter, and realizing I couldn't get out to my studio. I couldn't walk the dog. I couldn't do much of anything except read, and as I mentioned, even that started to lose its appeal. 

And that’s when I think this... this grayness really settled in. I kept telling myself, "Once the knee heals, once you're back on your feet, the fog will lift." And the knee did heal, eventually. I mean, it still aches when it rains, but I can walk perfectly fine now. But the fog... the fog never lifted. It just stayed right there, long after the physical therapy appointments ended. So yes, it’s been a little over three years now that I’ve been carrying this around with me. Three years of just... going through the motions.

Like that time back in '98 when I decided not to take that partnership offer at the firm because I thought the commute would be too taxing, and then the firm ended up expanding massively... but that's just life, isn't it? As for my current situation, this... this muted feeling... I don't feel guilty about it. It's more of a frustration, really. A profound, quiet frustration. I know my wife gets worried, and I suppose I feel a twinge of regret that I can't be the lively companion she married, the one who used to plan all those hiking trips and surprise her with weekend getaways to bed and breakfasts up the coast. But guilt implies I feel like I'm doing this on purpose, or that it's a moral failing on my part. And I don't think it is. I'm trying, you know? I'm going out to the studio every morning at nine, I'm sitting down for dinner, I'm attempting to read my biographies. I'm doing everything I'm supposed to do to keep the engine running, so to speak. It's just that the engine isn't producing any power. So no, I don't sit in my leather chair reproaching myself. I just sit there wondering why the effort I'm putting in isn't yielding any sort of return.

doctor.question: Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (whether there are any activities the patient still enjoys or looks forward to). This symptom is not present in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, that’s the rub, isn't it? I’ve been racking my brain trying to find something—anything, really—that sparks that old feeling. You’d think, being retired, having all this free time and a comfortable pension, I’d be jumping out of bed to seize the day. 

Take my daughter, for example. She comes over most Sunday afternoons with our two grandchildren. Now, any grandfather worth his salt is supposed to look forward to that all week, right? My wife spends two days prepping for it, baking cookies, getting a roast ready—the whole house smells like rosemary and garlic by noon on Sunday. And the kids, they come bursting through the front door, the dog gets all riled up and starts barking, it’s this whole grand production. It’s exactly the sort of family picture I worked all those decades at the firm to be able to sit back and enjoy in my twilight years. 

But... if I'm being completely honest with you, and I suppose that's why I'm sitting in this office... I don't actually look forward to it. I see it marked on the calendar in the kitchen, and instead of anticipation, I just feel... well, tired, I suppose. I think about the noise, and the sheer amount of energy it’s going to require to sit there and smile and ask the boys about their little league games and pretend I'm engaged. I love them, obviously. I'm not a monster, I care for my family deeply. But that actual feeling of joy? That little flutter in your chest when you know something good is about to happen? I just don't have it. 

And it's the same for the little things, too. I used to love just walking down the driveway to get the mail. I'd enjoy the crisp morning air, maybe chat with Bob, our postman—he's been on our route for fifteen years, good man, his son just graduated from state college. But now, even walking down the driveway is just a chore. It's just another thing I have to do. Not for Sunday dinners, not for my woodworking, not even for a quiet evening on the porch with a glass of iced tea. It’s all just... tasks on a list now. Boxes to check before the sun goes down. So, no, to answer your question. I really can't think of a single thing I genuinely look forward to anymore.

patient.answer:
Well, yes. Yes, I do. But it’s... it’s a peculiar kind of tired, if I’m being precise. It’s not that I’m bedridden or incapable of functioning, so please don't get the wrong impression. I still get up at the same time every morning. I still do my share of the household errands—I do the grocery shopping on Tuesdays and Thursdays, for instance. And, as I mentioned before, I still go out to the garage and tinker with my woodworking projects. I go through the motions. But the energy it takes to do these things... it’s entirely disproportionate to the task itself. 

Let me give you an example. It used to be effortless. Or if my wife wants to go to one of those community events they hold downtown in the square—the art fairs or the farmer's market—just walking through the event, navigating the stalls and the people... by the time we get back to the car, I feel like I've just argued a grueling three-week trial. 

And the frustrating part is that resting doesn't seem to cure it. I’ll come home from one of these outings, sit down in my recliner in the den, and try to sleep it off. But even if I do manage to drift off, a nap doesn’t really fix it. I wake up feeling just as heavy and drained as I did before I closed my eyes. It’s this persistent, bone-deep weariness that just follows me around, no matter what I’m doing or how much I rest.

Doctor, I... honestly, I am completely baffled as to why we are circling back to this yet again. I feel like we are trapped in some sort of deposition where the opposing counsel just keeps asking the same question in slightly different ways, hoping I'll somehow give a different answer. 

Have I lost interest in activities I used to enjoy? Yes, doctor. I have. We've spent the better part of this session discussing exactly that. I told you about the Sunday dinners with my daughter and the grandchildren. I told you about my woodworking studio out in the garage, and how I just sit there staring at the tools. I told you about the morning walks to the mailbox to see Bob. I walked you through the minutiae of grinding the Ethiopian coffee beans and reading the editorial section of the morning paper. 

So, yes, the interest is gone. The enjoyment is gone. It's all just... flat. It's a chore. I don't know how many different ways I can describe this overarching grayness to you. It feels like I've exhausted every possible example from my daily life, from the major family events down to the thirty seconds it takes to grind coffee beans. I'm really trying to be cooperative here, but I'm struggling to understand what nuance you're looking for that I haven't already provided three or four times now.

doctor.question: Have you been having trouble sleeping?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble sleeping (insomnia or hypersomnia), which is not covered by any of the symptoms in my profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. Sleep itself isn't the problem, not in the sense of... well, you know, tossing and turning or staring at the ceiling until three in the morning. I don't have insomnia, if that's what you're getting at. 

I actually keep a very strict schedule. I always have. Forty years in corporate litigation will drill that into you—you have to be disciplined with your time or the work just swallows you whole. So, my wife and I, we head up to the bedroom around ten o'clock every night. She usually reads one of her mystery novels for a bit—she goes through those paperbacks like water, I swear she buys three new ones every week at that little used bookstore on Elm Street. I might look over some notes for my mentoring sessions, or just close my eyes. And usually, by ten-thirty, the lights are out and I'm asleep. 

I sleep through the night, for the most part. Occasional trip to the bathroom, as you'd expect at my age, but I go right back to sleep. And I wake up at six-thirty, sharp, every morning. The alarm goes off, and I'm awake. 

So the mechanics of sleeping are perfectly intact. I get my eight hours. It's just that, as I was trying to explain earlier when we were talking about my energy levels... the sleep doesn't seem to *do* anything anymore. It used to be restorative, you know? You have a long day, you get a good night's sleep, and you wake up feeling refreshed and ready to tackle the next set of depositions or whatever was on the docket. Now, I sleep the full eight hours, I dream, I wake up, and I feel exactly as heavy and drained as I did when I laid down. It's like plugging in a phone overnight and waking up to find the battery is still at ten percent. 

But to answer your specific question about having *trouble* sleeping... no. Getting to sleep and staying asleep isn't an issue at all. I just wish the sleep actually accomplished something.

So our meals are very structured—lots of grilled fish, olive oil, leafy greens. We used to go out to dinner at least twice a week when I was still at the firm, usually to this Italian place near the courthouse, Luigi's. I'd always get the veal parmesan, which I'm sure wasn't doing my arteries any favors. But now, it's mostly home-cooked meals. 

And as I mentioned, the enjoyment of the food is completely gone. I sit down to dinner, and it just tastes like... well, like cardboard, quite frankly. I chew, I swallow, I go through the motions because I know I need the sustenance, and because my wife went to the trouble of preparing it. I don't want to upset her by refusing to eat. She puts so much effort into finding these recipes—she even started growing her own herbs in little pots on the kitchen windowsill. Basil, thyme, rosemary. She’s very proud of them. 

So, I eat what's put in front of me. I clean my plate, just like I always have. The mechanics of eating, much like the mechanics of sleeping, haven't changed. I just don't get any satisfaction from it anymore. But to answer your question, no, the scale hasn't budged. My suits all still fit exactly the same way they did when I retired. I suppose that's a small mercy, not having to go out and buy a whole new wardrobe, but... well, no, no weight loss to speak of.

I'll exchange pleasantries with the mail carrier if we happen to cross paths, though as I mentioned earlier, even that morning walk has lost its appeal. But beyond the absolute bare minimum, yes, I've pulled back considerably. 

Take my mentoring, for example. I used to really enjoy that. Working with the junior associates, reviewing their briefs, teaching them the finer points of deposition strategy... it gave me a sense of purpose. I was passing the torch, so to speak. I had a regular group of three or four young lawyers I'd meet with every Tuesday afternoon at this little coffee shop near the firm. But I just... I couldn't keep up the facade. Sitting there, trying to muster enthusiasm for contract disputes when everything just feels so gray and heavy... I eventually just told them I needed to take an indefinite hiatus. I said it was for personal reasons, which I suppose is true enough.

And it's not just the professional stuff. We used to be quite active in the community. My wife and I were on the organizing committee for the annual summer festival at the park down the street. I used to coordinate the local music gatherings—booking the jazz quartets, making sure the staging was right. I haven't been to a single committee meeting in months. I just let my wife go on her own, or she skips it entirely, which makes me feel guilty, but I just can't bring myself to sit in a room with twelve other people debating whether to hire a face painter or a balloon artist. 

Even our travel plans... we had talked about taking a river cruise through Europe this fall. The Danube, I think it was. We had the brochures sitting on the kitchen counter for weeks. But the thought of navigating airports, making small talk with other couples at dinner, pretending to be awestruck by castles... I just couldn't do it. I told her we should postpone. 

So, yes, my weeks are much, much smaller than they used to be. My world has basically shrunk down to the walls of my house. And even then, I find myself retreating to the garage or the den just to be alone. It's just easier that way. You don't have to pretend when you're by yourself.

No, no. Heavens, no. I want to be very clear about that right out of the gate. I haven't had any thoughts of... of harming myself, or wishing I wouldn't wake up, or anything of that nature.

I suppose when you stack all of that together on a notepad, it probably sounds like someone who has just given up completely. But there is a very distinct line, in my mind anyway, between feeling like a drained battery and actually wanting to... well, to throw the battery away entirely, if you follow my meaning. 

I spent forty years in corporate litigation, as I mentioned before. You see a lot of people in incredibly high-stress situations, and sadly, over the decades, I've known a couple of colleagues who did go down that very dark path. There was a senior partner back in the late eighties—brilliant man, absolutely brilliant mind for antitrust law—who just couldn't take it anymore. I saw firsthand what that did to his family. The absolute, unimaginable devastation it left behind for his wife and his children. The messy aftermath of it all. 

I could never, ever do that to my wife. She’s... well, she’s the one keeping our routine going right now, isn't she? Cooking those Mediterranean meals, tending to her little basil and thyme plants on the windowsill, trying to keep things normal. To inflict that kind of trauma on her? Unthinkable. Absolutely unthinkable. I take my commitments very seriously, and my marriage is the most important one I have. 

So, no. I don't wish I were dead. I just wish... I just wish I felt *alive* again, the way I used to. Right now, I'm just enduring. I wake up at six-thirty sharp, I go through the motions, I eat what's put in front of me, and I fulfill my basic obligations. It's a very flat, gray sort of endurance. Just putting one foot in front of the other. But it *is* endurance. I have absolutely no intention of cutting it short. I suppose I'm just waiting for the color to come back to things, even if I don't quite know how to make that happen right now. But as far as harming myself goes, no. Not at all.
